title: Give every plugin the host's one quota

blocks.text: The integration host runs partner plugins, and every plugin's calls to the partner API must come out of one budget, `PluginHost.Quota.INSTANCE`. Each plugin gets a class loader of its own, and that loader is meant to look in the plugin's jar first, so a plugin runs with the library versions it bundles. Plugins are compiled against the host API (the nested types of `PluginHost`), and their build copies that API into the jar.
The partner reports that the host goes over its budget whenever more than one plugin is installed. Finish the two `TODO`s in `src/main/java/practice/PluginHost.java`, in the plugin loader:

items: `loadClass(name, resolve)`: which loader defines each class a plugin asks for;
`sharedWithHost(name)`: which classes a plugin must get from the host, whatever its jar holds.

blocks.text: When you're done, every plugin draws on the host's one quota, and two plugins never share the static state of their own classes. About twelve lines in total.
The tests build each plugin from a directory that holds both the plugin classes and the host's classes, as a plugin jar does.

cases.says: a plugin loaded through its own loader runs and is usable as the host's Plugin type
calls made by two separately loaded plugins are taken from the host's one Quota, although each plugin jar carries a copy of the class
two loads of the same plugin class get separate static state, because each plugin's own classes come from its own loader

origin.section: Each Class Loader Has Its Own Singleton, Enum Included

concepts: A class is identified by its name and its defining loader, so two loaders that define the same singleton class hold two instances and two states, and casting one to the other's type fails.
A singleton stays one per process only when one shared parent loader defines it; a child-first loader must send the shared API to the parent.
